title: Life recovers after the K–Pg extinction
summary: In the first million years after the asteroid impact, forests and mammals rebuilt ecosystems, as recorded at Corral Bluffs, Colorado.
description: The end-Cretaceous extinction removed roughly three-quarters of species, including all non-avian dinosaurs. Fossils from Corral Bluffs near Colorado Springs, dated by volcanic ash and magnetic reversals, show fern-dominated landscapes giving way to palm and walnut-family forests, mammals growing markedly larger within a few hundred thousand years, and legumes appearing about 700,000 years after the impact. In the oceans, plankton communities and the flux of organic carbon to the deep sea took longer to recover, on the order of one to several million years. The rapid radiation of placental mammals and birds during the Paleocene laid the foundations of the modern biosphere.

title: Titanoboa, the largest known snake
summary: A boa relative about 13 m long lived in the hot Paleocene rainforests of what is now the Cerrejón coal mine in northern Colombia.
description: Titanoboa cerrejonensis was described in 2009 from vertebrae found in the Cerrejón Formation of La Guajira, Colombia, which also preserves one of the oldest known Neotropical rainforests. Estimated at around 13 m long and over a tonne in weight, it is the largest snake known from the fossil record. It shared its swampy habitat with giant turtles and crocodile relatives. Its describers used its size to infer tropical temperatures of about 30–34 °C, an inference other researchers have questioned because body size depends on more than climate.

title: Paleocene–Eocene Thermal Maximum
summary: A massive release of carbon warmed the planet by about 5–8 °C within a few thousand years, acidifying the oceans and reshaping life.
description: At the Paleocene–Eocene boundary several thousand gigatonnes of carbon entered the ocean and atmosphere, marked by a sharp carbon-isotope excursion in sediments worldwide, including the boundary stratotype at Dababiya, Egypt. Global temperatures rose by roughly 5–8 °C, the deep ocean acidified and 30–50% of deep-sea benthic foraminifera species went extinct. On land, the earliest true primates (euprimates) and even-toed and odd-toed hoofed mammals appeared and spread rapidly across North America, Europe and Asia. The carbon source is still debated, with volcanism in the North Atlantic Igneous Province, methane hydrates and thawing permafrost or peat as leading candidates. Lasting roughly 150,000–200,000 years, the event is widely studied as an analogue for modern warming.

title: Silurian hypothesis: a pre-human industrial civilisation?
dateLabel: Thought experiment; PETM (c. 56 million years ago) as a test case
summary: A 2018 thought experiment asked whether an industrial civilisation millions of years ago would still be detectable, using events like the PETM as test cases.
description: In 2018 climate scientist Gavin Schmidt and astrophysicist Adam Frank published 'The Silurian hypothesis', named after the reptilian beings of the television series Doctor Who, asking what geological traces an industrial civilisation would leave after millions of years. They noted that such a signature, including rapid carbon-isotope shifts, warming, ocean deoxygenation and unusual pollutants, could resemble natural hyperthermal events such as the Paleocene–Eocene Thermal Maximum. The authors stated plainly that they did not believe such a civilisation existed; the paper aimed to sharpen how scientists might recognise industrial signatures on Earth or other planets. Popular media have sometimes repeated the idea as a serious claim of a lost pre-human civilisation.
mainstreamView: There is no evidence of any pre-human technological civilisation. The PETM's carbon release unfolded over thousands of years, more slowly than today's emissions, and is attributed to natural sources such as North Atlantic volcanism and carbon-cycle feedbacks (the exact mix is still debated); no artefacts, synthetic compounds or anomalous isotopes have been found in Paleocene–Eocene sediments. Schmidt and Frank themselves framed the idea as a thought experiment, not a claim.

title: India collides with Asia; the Himalaya rise
summary: The Indian plate began colliding with Eurasia, closing the Tethys Ocean and starting to build the Himalaya and the Tibetan Plateau.
description: After moving north at up to about 15–20 cm per year following its separation from Gondwana, the Indian plate made first contact with Asia along what is now the Indus–Yarlung suture zone in southern Tibet. Many estimates place initial contact between about 60 and 50 million years ago, with several recent sedimentary studies favouring about 60–55 million years ago, though proposals range as young as about 35 million years ago, partly depending on whether an intervening island arc or a stretched 'Greater India' collided first. The convergence continues today at about 4–5 cm per year. It raised the Himalaya and the Tibetan Plateau, strengthened the Asian monsoon and may have helped cool the planet by accelerating the chemical weathering that draws down carbon dioxide.

title: Lemuria: a sunken continent in the Indian Ocean?
dateLabel: Claimed lost continent; lemur ancestors reached Madagascar c. 60–50 million years ago
summary: A sunken Indian Ocean continent, proposed in 1864 to explain lemur-like primates in Madagascar and India, later became an occult myth; science rejects it.
description: In 1864 the zoologist Philip Sclater proposed a lost land bridge or continent, which he called Lemuria, to explain why lemurs and related primates were known from Madagascar and India but not from mainland Africa or the Middle East. In 1870 Ernst Haeckel suggested that it might have been the original home of humankind. After scientists abandoned the idea, it lived on in esoteric writings, notably Helena Blavatsky's The Secret Doctrine (1888), which made Lemuria the home of an ancient 'root race', and some Tamil revivalist writers identified it with Kumari Kandam, a legendary land swallowed by the sea. It remains popular in New Age and pseudohistorical literature.
mainstreamView: Plate tectonics and ocean-floor surveys rule out a sunken continent linking Madagascar and India. The two were joined within Gondwana until about 88 million years ago, long before lemurs existed, and the sea floor of the western Indian Ocean is mostly oceanic crust; only small continental fragments, such as the Seychelles and slivers buried beneath Mauritius, remain from the break-up. Genetic and fossil evidence indicates that lemurs descend from primates that crossed from Africa to Madagascar, most likely by rafting on floating vegetation, roughly 60–50 million years ago, while the lorises of India belong to a separate branch that spread through Africa and Asia over land.

title: Early Eocene Climatic Optimum
summary: The warmest sustained interval of the Cenozoic, when there were no large polar ice sheets and alligator relatives lived in the Arctic.
description: Between about 53 and 49 million years ago, atmospheric carbon dioxide was probably well above 1,000 ppm and global mean temperatures were perhaps 10–16 °C warmer than pre-industrial levels. Fossils from Ellesmere Island in the Canadian Arctic include alligator relatives, giant tortoises, snakes and hippo-like mammals living above 75°N alongside swamp forests of dawn redwood. Tropical sea-surface temperatures may have exceeded 35 °C. After the optimum, a long cooling trend began that eventually led to Antarctic glaciation.

title: Pakicetus and the first whales
summary: Wolf-sized, four-legged ancestors of whales lived along rivers and shallow seas in what is now northern Pakistan.
description: Pakicetus, described in 1981 by Philip Gingerich and Donald Russell from the Kala Chitta Hills of Pakistan, is among the earliest known cetaceans, a group descended from even-toed hoofed mammals and most closely related today to hippos. It was a land-dwelling, four-legged animal, but its ear bones already showed features unique to whales. Within about 10 million years the lineage passed through amphibious forms such as Ambulocetus and Rodhocetus to fully marine whales like Basilosaurus, whose tiny hind limbs are preserved at Wadi Al-Hitan in Egypt. The sequence is one of the best-documented evolutionary transitions in the fossil record.

title: Messel Pit fossils
summary: A volcanic crater lake near Darmstadt preserved Eocene mammals, birds and insects in extraordinary detail, down to fur and stomach contents.
description: The Messel Pit is an oil-shale deposit laid down in a maar lake that formed after a volcanic explosion about 48 million years ago, its fossil-bearing sediments accumulating over several hundred thousand years. Oxygen-poor bottom waters preserved complete skeletons with body outlines, feathers, the colours of beetles and the gut contents of early horses, bats, primates, crocodiles and birds. Saved from being turned into a landfill site, it became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1995. In 2009 the primate fossil 'Ida' (Darwinius masillae) was publicised as a human ancestor, but most researchers regard it as an adapiform more closely related to lemurs.

title: Early anthropoid primates of the Fayum
summary: Fossils from Egypt's Fayum Depression record early anthropoid primates near the ancestry of monkeys and apes, including the 30-million-year-old Aegyptopithecus.
description: The Jebel Qatrani Formation and older beds of the Fayum Depression, west of the Nile, have yielded the richest record of early anthropoids, the group that includes monkeys, apes and humans. Species such as Catopithecus and the cat-sized Aegyptopithecus, from about 30–29 million years ago, lived in warm, swampy forests and are thought to lie close to the common ancestry of Old World monkeys and apes. Older anthropoid-like primates from Asia, such as Eosimias from China, lead many researchers to favour an Asian origin for anthropoids followed by dispersal into Africa.

title: Monkeys and rodents raft to South America
summary: Ancestors of New World monkeys and caviomorph rodents crossed the then-narrower Atlantic from Africa, probably on floating vegetation.
description: South America was an island continent for most of the Cenozoic, yet monkeys and caviomorph rodents, the group that includes guinea pigs and capybaras, appear there suddenly in the Eocene. Their closest relatives lived in Africa, and fossils such as the primate Perupithecus from Santa Rosa in the Peruvian Amazon indicate that monkeys had arrived by about 36 million years ago, with rodents present by about 41 million years ago. The South Atlantic was then considerably narrower than today, and the leading explanation is accidental rafting on mats of vegetation, perhaps aided by islands and favourable currents. The exact age of the Santa Rosa beds remains uncertain.

title: Antarctica freezes: the Eocene–Oligocene transition
summary: Continental ice sheets spread across Antarctica within a few hundred thousand years as falling CO2 tipped Earth into an icehouse climate.
description: Across the Eocene–Oligocene transition, deep-sea oxygen-isotope records show a two-step shift that began about 34 million years ago and culminated in the Oi-1 event about 33.6 million years ago, reflecting the growth of a large East Antarctic ice sheet and global cooling. The ice probably nucleated on highlands such as the Gamburtsev Mountains and reached the coast within a few hundred thousand years, lowering sea level by tens of metres. Models and proxy records point to declining atmospheric CO2 as the main trigger, with the opening of the Drake Passage and the Tasmanian Gateway, which allowed the Antarctic Circumpolar Current to form, playing a supporting role whose timing is still debated. The transition marked Earth's shift from a greenhouse to the icehouse climate that persists today.

title: The Grande Coupure
summary: Europe's mammal fauna was abruptly reshaped as many endemic groups vanished and Asian immigrants such as rhinos and hamster-like rodents arrived.
description: The 'great break', named by Swiss palaeontologist Hans Georg Stehlin in 1910, is a major turnover of European mammals that Stehlin placed at the Eocene–Oligocene boundary; improved correlations now date it to the earliest Oligocene, shortly after the boundary and at about the time of the Oi-1 glaciation. Many endemic European groups, including most palaeotheres (relatives of horses) and adapiform primates, disappeared, while immigrants from Asia such as rhinoceroses, hamster-like rodents and beavers spread westwards. Falling sea level as Antarctic ice grew probably helped drain the Turgai Strait seaway that had separated Europe from Asia, and the cooler, drier climate favoured the newcomers. The sequence is especially well recorded in the fossil-rich phosphorite deposits of Quercy in southern France.

title: Ethiopian flood basalts and the East African Rift
summary: A mantle plume beneath Ethiopia poured out vast basalt lavas and helped drive the rifting that is slowly splitting East Africa apart.
description: Around 30 million years ago the arrival of the Afar mantle plume produced the Ethiopian and Yemeni flood basalts, locally up to 2 km thick and covering hundreds of thousands of square kilometres, within about a million years. Rifting followed as the Red Sea and Gulf of Aden began to open, and the East African Rift, whose oldest basins in northern Kenya and southern Ethiopia date back to the Eocene, developed through Ethiopia and Kenya over the following tens of millions of years. Uplift of the East African plateaus and the rift's chain of lakes and volcanoes reshaped the region's climate and landscapes. Sediments accumulating in the rift basins preserve much of the hominin fossil record.

title: Paraceratherium, giant of Oligocene Asia
summary: A hornless rhinoceros relative almost 5 m tall at the shoulder, among the largest land mammals ever, browsed the woodlands of Oligocene Asia.
description: Paraceratherium, also known by the names Indricotherium and Baluchitherium, lived across Central and South Asia during the Oligocene. Estimates suggest it weighed around 15–20 tonnes and could browse leaves some 7 m above the ground. Fossils were first collected in the Bugti Hills of Balochistan, Pakistan, by the geologist Guy Pilgrim in 1907–1908, with further finds there by Clive Forster-Cooper in 1910, and later in Kazakhstan and Mongolia, including by Roy Chapman Andrews's expeditions. Its disappearance by the end of the Oligocene may relate to changing habitats and perhaps the arrival of elephant relatives from Africa.

title: The Oligocene drowning of Zealandia
summary: Most of the sunken continent of Zealandia lay under the sea in the late Oligocene; whether New Zealand was ever completely submerged is debated.
description: Zealandia, a largely submerged continental fragment that rifted away from Gondwana between about 85 and 60 million years ago, subsided slowly through the Paleogene. By the late Oligocene, widespread marine limestones show that its land area had shrunk to a small fraction of today's New Zealand. Some geologists proposed in the 2000s that the land vanished entirely, which would imply that all of New Zealand's land life arrived later by dispersal across the sea. Renewed uplift along the Pacific–Australian plate boundary from the Miocene onwards raised the islands again.
mainstreamView: Most researchers think small islands probably persisted, because some ancient lineages, such as the tuatara's relatives and leiopelmatid frogs, appear to have been present continuously, and Miocene fossils of the St Bathans fauna include old endemic groups. The geological record alone cannot rule out total submergence, so the question remains open.

title: Riversleigh: Australia's Miocene rainforests
summary: Limestones in north-west Queensland preserve marsupial lions, early kangaroos, a toothed platypus and many bats from lush forests.
description: The Riversleigh fossil field, inscribed with Naracoorte as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1994, records Australian ecosystems across the last 25 million years or so. Its Oligocene and Miocene limestones, formed in pools and caves within a once-wet rainforest, contain marsupial lions, early kangaroos, thylacines, the toothed platypus Obdurodon and numerous bats. Younger layers document the drying of the continent and the shift towards the open woodlands and arid habitats of modern Australia.

title: Megalodon, the largest predatory shark
summary: Otodus megalodon, a shark that probably exceeded 15 m in length and fed on whales, roamed warm seas worldwide until about 3.6 million years ago.
description: Megalodon is known mainly from its teeth, up to about 18 cm long, and from a few partial vertebral columns, so its size and body shape remain uncertain; estimates of maximum length range from about 14 to more than 20 m. Once classed with the great white shark, it is now placed in the extinct family Otodontidae. Its fossils occur worldwide, including at Calvert Cliffs in Maryland, and bite marks on fossil whale bones show that it attacked large marine mammals. It disappeared by about 3.6 million years ago; cooling oceans, changes in the distribution of its whale prey and competition with great white sharks and predatory sperm whales are thought to have contributed, though their relative importance is debated.

title: Grasslands spread and horses become grazers
summary: As climates cooled and dried, open grass-dominated habitats spread, and many mammals evolved teeth and legs suited to grazing.
description: Grasses originated in the Cretaceous but remained minor parts of mostly forested landscapes for tens of millions of years. Fossil phytoliths and ancient soils show that open, grass-dominated habitats became widespread on the North American Great Plains by the early Miocene, about 20 million years ago, with comparable expansions in Eurasia. Grazing mammals responded: horses such as Merychippus evolved high-crowned teeth to cope with abrasive grass and grit and longer legs for running in open country, and similar adaptations appeared in rhinos, camels and antelopes. The spread of grasslands transformed food webs, fire regimes and the carbon cycle.

title: Proconsul, an early ape
summary: Tailless, monkey-like apes lived in the forests of early Miocene East Africa; Mary Leakey found a famous skull on Rusinga Island in 1948.
description: Proconsul is one of the best-known early hominoids, the group that includes apes and humans. Its fossils, mostly from Kenya and Uganda, show a mixture of traits: like modern apes it lacked a tail, but it moved on all fours along branches more like a monkey. The skull found by Mary Leakey on Rusinga Island in Lake Victoria in 1948 was the first fossil ape skull ever discovered. It was long known as Proconsul africanus and later as P. heseloni, and since 2015 many researchers have placed it and the other Rusinga fossils in the closely related genus Ekembo. Africa's early Miocene forests supported a diversity of such apes before some spread into Eurasia around 16–17 million years ago.

title: Middle Miocene warmth and the Columbia River basalts
summary: Earth warmed for about two million years as huge Columbia River lava flows erupted, before cooling around 14 million years ago enlarged Antarctic ice.
description: During the Middle Miocene Climatic Optimum, global temperatures rose to several degrees above pre-industrial levels, warm forests extended to high latitudes and the Antarctic ice sheet shrank and fluctuated strongly. The warmth coincided with the eruption of the Columbia River Basalt Group in the north-western United States, some 170,000–210,000 km³ of lava, most of it erupted between about 16.7 and 15.9 million years ago, and many researchers link the warming to volcanic carbon dioxide, although the size of that contribution is debated. The optimum gave way to the Middle Miocene Climate Transition, in which deep-sea oxygen-isotope records show cooling and the expansion of the East Antarctic ice sheet, culminating around 13.9 million years ago. Cooling then continued, with interruptions, towards the ice ages of the Quaternary.

title: Miocene apes spread across Eurasia
summary: Apes left Africa and diversified across Europe and Asia, including Sivapithecus of the Siwalik Hills, a probable relative of orangutans.
description: From around 16–17 million years ago, warm and forested conditions allowed apes to spread from Africa into Eurasia, where they diversified into forms such as Griphopithecus in Turkey, Dryopithecus and Pierolapithecus in Spain and France, Ouranopithecus in Greece and Sivapithecus in the Siwalik Hills of Pakistan and India. Sivapithecus, known from about 12.5 to 8.5 million years ago, shares distinctive facial features with orangutans and is widely considered part of their lineage. Some researchers argue that the ancestors of African great apes and humans evolved in Europe and later returned to Africa, while others favour continuous African ancestry. As climates cooled and forests retreated in the late Miocene, most Eurasian apes died out.

title: C4 grasslands expand
summary: Grasses using the efficient C4 photosynthetic pathway spread rapidly across warm lowlands, a shift first recorded in the ancient soils of Pakistan.
description: Carbon isotopes in ancient soils and in the tooth enamel of grazing mammals show a marked shift between about 8 and 6 million years ago, first documented in the Siwalik deposits of Pakistan and then in parts of Africa and the Americas. C4 grasses concentrate CO2 inside their leaves, which gives them an advantage in hot, seasonally dry climates and possibly at lower CO2 levels. The causes, including declining CO2, increasing aridity and seasonality and more frequent fire, are still debated, and the timing varied between regions. The expansion created the tropical savannas in which many large mammals, and later hominins, evolved.

title: Sahelanthropus tchadensis ('Toumaï')
summary: A skull found in the Djurab Desert of Chad in 2001 may belong to one of the earliest known members of the human lineage.
description: Nicknamed Toumaï, 'hope of life' in the local Daza language, the cranium was found in 2001 by a team led by Michel Brunet and described in 2002. It combines a small, chimpanzee-sized brain with a relatively short face, small canines and a forward-placed foramen magnum, features its describers interpreted as signs of the human lineage and possibly of upright walking. Its age of about 7 million years, close to genetic estimates for the human–chimpanzee split, comes from cosmogenic nuclide dating and the associated fauna. Its discovery some 2,500 km west of the East African Rift showed that early hominins were not confined to East Africa.
mainstreamView: Many palaeoanthropologists accept Sahelanthropus as a possible early hominin, but this is contested. A femur found with the remains has been interpreted both as evidence of habitual bipedalism and as that of a quadrupedal ape, and some researchers consider the species a stem ape that lived before the human–chimpanzee split.

title: Aquatic ape hypothesis
dateLabel: Proposed for c. 7–5 million years ago
summary: The claim that human ancestors passed through a semi-aquatic phase that shaped bipedalism, hairlessness and body fat; rejected by mainstream science.
description: Anticipated by the German pathologist Max Westenhöfer in 1942, proposed independently by marine biologist Alister Hardy in 1960 and popularised by the writer Elaine Morgan from 1972, the hypothesis proposes that early hominins spent part of their evolution wading, swimming and diving for food in coastal or flooded habitats. Proponents argue that this explains a cluster of human traits, including upright walking, loss of body hair, a layer of fat beneath the skin, voluntary breath control and a descended larynx. Some proponents pointed to the Afar region of Ethiopia, thought to have been partly flooded by the sea in the late Miocene, as a possible setting. The idea attracted public attention through books and radio documentaries presented by David Attenborough, but it has not been adopted by palaeoanthropologists.
mainstreamView: Fossils from this period, such as Sahelanthropus, Orrorin and Ardipithecus, come from woodland and mosaic habitats and show no aquatic adaptations, and the cited traits evolved at different times rather than as a package: bipedalism appeared millions of years before reduced body hair or large brains. Each trait has well-supported alternative explanations, such as hairlessness and sweating for shedding heat during activity on open ground. Researchers do accept that later hominins exploited shorelines, lakes and aquatic foods, but not that humans passed through a semi-aquatic evolutionary stage.

title: Orrorin tugenensis ('Millennium Man')
summary: Fossils from Kenya's Tugen Hills, found in 2000, include thigh bones suggesting this early hominin walked upright about 6 million years ago.
description: Orrorin tugenensis was described in 2001 by a team led by Brigitte Senut and Martin Pickford from about 20 fossils recovered from the Lukeino Formation, dated to roughly 6.1–5.7 million years ago. The shape of its femur, particularly the neck and the distribution of bone within it, indicates that it walked on two legs, while its arm and finger bones suggest it still climbed trees. Its small teeth with thick enamel differ from those of chimpanzees. Because the remains are fragmentary, its exact relationship to later hominins remains uncertain.

title: Messinian salinity crisis
summary: Cut off from the Atlantic, the Mediterranean partly evaporated, leaving salt layers more than a kilometre thick beneath its floor.
description: Late in the Miocene, tectonic uplift around the Gibraltar arc restricted and eventually severed the marine gateways between the Atlantic and the Mediterranean, and evaporation outpaced the inflow from rivers and rain. Over about 640,000 years, more than a million cubic kilometres of gypsum and halite accumulated, in places over 2 km thick and amounting to around 6% of the salt dissolved in the world ocean. Rivers such as the Nile and the Rhône cut deep canyons as their base level fell. How far the sea level dropped, and whether the deep basins became largely dry salt flats or stayed filled with deep brine, are still debated.

title: Zanclean flood refills the Mediterranean
summary: Atlantic water broke through at Gibraltar and refilled the Mediterranean, marking the start of the Pliocene epoch.
description: The Messinian salinity crisis ended abruptly at the Miocene–Pliocene boundary, when fully marine conditions returned across the Mediterranean. A widely cited 2009 model suggested that water eroding a channel across the Gibraltar sill could have reached flows of about 100 million cubic metres per second, refilling the basin within a few months to two years. An eroded channel some 200 km long beneath the Strait and the Alboran Sea is interpreted as the flood's path, and chaotic deposits off south-east Sicily have been attributed to a cascade over the Malta Escarpment.
mainstreamView: The reconnection of the Mediterranean to the Atlantic at 5.33 million years ago is established, but the speed of refilling is debated. Some researchers favour a catastrophic megaflood; others interpret the evidence as a more gradual or stepwise reconnection, with the basin already partly refilled during the brackish 'Lago-Mare' phase that preceded it.

title: Ardipithecus and 'Ardi'
summary: A partial skeleton from Aramis, Ethiopia, reveals a hominin that walked upright on the ground yet kept a grasping big toe for climbing.
description: Ardipithecus ramidus was first described in 1994, and a detailed study of a partial female skeleton nicknamed 'Ardi' was published in 2009 by Tim White and colleagues. Dated to about 4.4 million years ago, it had a chimpanzee-sized brain, small canines and a pelvis and foot that combined adaptations for upright walking with an opposable big toe. Its associated plants and animals point to a wooded habitat, challenging the idea that bipedalism arose on the open savanna. An older species, Ardipithecus kadabba, is known from about 5.8–5.2 million years ago; how both relate to later australopiths is debated.

title: Laetoli footprints
summary: Hominins walked across damp volcanic ash in Tanzania, leaving the oldest known trackway of upright, human-like walking.
description: Mary Leakey's team first identified footprints at Laetoli in 1976, and in 1978 uncovered the main hominin trails at Site G, preserved in a layer of volcanic ash that had been dampened by rain and then hardened; the ash was long attributed to the nearby Sadiman volcano, a source now questioned. The prints, in a trail about 27 m long, show a big toe in line with the other toes and a heel-strike gait broadly like that of modern humans, and are usually attributed to Australopithecus afarensis. Tracks of hares, birds and other animals were preserved alongside them. In 2021 a separate set of prints at the site was reinterpreted as having been made by a different, unidentified hominin.

title: Forbidden Archeology: modern humans in the Pliocene?
dateLabel: Claimed Pliocene, c. 4–3 million years ago
summary: A 1993 book claimed that anatomically modern humans lived millions of years ago, citing old finds such as Italy's Castenedolo skeletons; scientists reject it.
description: In Forbidden Archeology, Michael Cremo and Richard L. Thompson collected nineteenth- and early twentieth-century reports of human bones and artefacts in very old strata and argued that scientists had suppressed evidence that modern humans have existed for millions of years, a view the authors linked to Hindu Vedic chronology. A frequently cited case is Castenedolo near Brescia, where the geologist Giuseppe Ragazzoni reported human skeletons in Pliocene marine clays in 1860 and 1880. The book also invokes eoliths, naturally broken flints once claimed as tools, and various anomalous footprints and objects.
mainstreamView: Mainstream scholars reject the claim because the cases rely on old excavations with poor stratigraphic control and have been re-examined: chemical tests on the Castenedolo bones match recent rather than Pliocene remains, indicating later burials dug into older clays, and eoliths are explained by natural fracturing. The fossil, genetic and archaeological records consistently show that Homo sapiens arose in Africa within roughly the last 300,000 years from earlier hominins that were anatomically very different.

title: Lomekwi 3: the oldest known stone tools
summary: Large stone cores and flakes from West Turkana, Kenya, reported in 2015, predate the earliest known members of the genus Homo.
description: Work led by Sonia Harmand at the Lomekwi 3 site, west of Lake Turkana, recovered about 150 knapped stones, including heavy cores, flakes and possible anvils; only around 20 were excavated in place from sediments dated to about 3.3 million years ago, and the rest were collected from the surface. If correct, the find pushes the origin of stone toolmaking back some 700,000 years before the Oldowan and implies that australopiths or Kenyanthropus, rather than Homo, were the makers. The artefacts are cruder than Oldowan tools and were probably made by striking cores against an anvil or using them as hammers. Cut-marked animal bones from Dikika, Ethiopia, about 3.4 million years old, also hint at early tool use, though their interpretation is disputed.
mainstreamView: Many archaeologists accept Lomekwi 3 as evidence of pre-Oldowan toolmaking, but critics have questioned whether all the artefacts truly come from the dated layers rather than younger deposits, and comparable sites have not yet been found. The Oldowan, from about 2.6 million years ago, remains the earliest widely accepted stone-tool tradition.

title: Lucy (Australopithecus afarensis)
summary: A 40% complete skeleton found at Hadar, Ethiopia, in 1974 showed that hominins walked upright long before their brains grew large.
description: Discovered on 24 November 1974 by Donald Johanson and Tom Gray, the skeleton AL 288-1 was nicknamed Lucy after the Beatles song 'Lucy in the Sky with Diamonds', played at the expedition camp that night. About 1.1 m tall, with a brain only slightly larger than a chimpanzee's, she had a pelvis and knees adapted for bipedal walking while retaining long, curved fingers suited to climbing. Her species, Australopithecus afarensis, lived in East Africa from about 3.9 to 2.9 million years ago and is known from hundreds of specimens. Lucy remains one of the most famous fossils in the world and is held at the National Museum of Ethiopia in Addis Ababa.

title: The Isthmus of Panama forms
summary: A land bridge built by volcanic arcs and plate collision joined North and South America and separated the Atlantic from the Pacific.
description: The collision of the Panama arc with north-western South America gradually narrowed the Central American Seaway over millions of years. Marine fossils, sediment cores and ocean chemistry indicate that the last deep-water connection closed by about 3 million years ago and that a continuous land bridge existed by around 2.8 million years ago. The closure reorganised ocean circulation, strengthening the Gulf Stream, and enabled the Great American Biotic Interchange; its once widely assumed role in triggering Northern Hemisphere glaciation is now debated. A 2015 study argued for closure as early as 13–15 million years ago, but most researchers favour the younger date for full emergence.

title: The Taung Child and Australopithecus africanus
summary: A child's skull from a South African limestone quarry, described by Raymond Dart in 1925, was the first australopith fossil to be recognised.
description: Quarry workers at the Buxton Limeworks near Taung blasted the fossil out in 1924, and the anatomist Raymond Dart named it Australopithecus africanus, 'southern ape of Africa', in Nature in February 1925. The skull of a child about three or four years old combined a small, ape-sized brain with human-like teeth and a forward-placed foramen magnum, which Dart took as evidence of upright walking. Leading British anatomists rejected his claim that it was a human ancestor, partly because they expected an early large brain like that of the fraudulent Piltdown Man, which was not exposed as a hoax until 1953. Robert Broom's finds of adult australopiths at Sterkfontein from 1936 and of the robust Paranthropus robustus at Kromdraai in 1938 helped vindicate Dart. Damage to the eye sockets suggests that the child was killed by a large bird of prey, and the cave deposits are hard to date, with most estimates centring on about 2.8 million years ago.

title: Great American Biotic Interchange
summary: Mammals crossed the new land bridge both ways: armadillos and ground sloths went north while cats, bears, horses and camels went south.
description: Earlier island-hopping brought ground sloths to North America and raccoon relatives to South America from around 9–7 million years ago, but the interchange peaked once a continuous land bridge formed around 2.7 million years ago. North American migrants such as sabre-toothed cats, bears, deer, camelids (ancestors of llamas) and horses spread through South America, while glyptodonts, giant ground sloths, armadillos, porcupines, opossums and terror birds moved north. Northern mammal lineages became far more successful in South America than the reverse, and many of South America's endemic groups, such as its native hoofed mammals, later declined. The interchange shaped the present-day fauna of both continents.

title: Oldowan stone tools
summary: Hominins at Gona, Ethiopia, began systematically striking sharp flakes from stone cores, starting the Oldowan toolmaking tradition.
description: Named after Olduvai Gorge in Tanzania, where Louis and Mary Leakey documented them, Oldowan tools consist of simple cores, choppers and sharp flakes used for cutting meat, processing plants and breaking bones for marrow. The oldest securely dated assemblages, from Gona and Ledi-Geraru in Ethiopia, are about 2.6 million years old, and finds at Nyayanga, Kenya, may be as old as 3 million years. Although long associated with early Homo, the earliest Oldowan tools may also have been made by Paranthropus or late australopiths. The tradition lasted for more than a million years and spread with early humans into Asia and Europe.

title: The Pleistocene ice ages begin
summary: Large ice sheets began repeatedly growing and shrinking across the Northern Hemisphere, opening the Quaternary period of ice ages.
description: After a gradual cooling through the Pliocene, ice sheets expanded markedly over North America, Greenland and Eurasia around 2.7 million years ago, and the base of the Quaternary period is defined at 2.58 million years ago, close to the Gauss–Matuyama magnetic reversal. From then on, glacial and interglacial periods alternated, paced by cyclic changes in Earth's orbit and axial tilt (Milankovitch cycles), at first roughly every 41,000 years. During the largest glaciations of the last million years, ice up to 3–4 km thick covered Canada and northern Europe and sea level fell by more than 100 m, exposing land bridges such as Beringia; the earlier 41,000-year glacials were generally smaller. The relative importance of declining CO2, changing ocean gateways and mountain uplift in starting the ice ages is still investigated.

title: Homo habilis and the earliest Homo
summary: Named in 1964 from fossils at Olduvai Gorge, the 'handy man' had a larger brain than australopiths and is linked to early stone tools.
description: Louis Leakey, Phillip Tobias and John Napier named Homo habilis in 1964 from fossils found at Olduvai Gorge, Tanzania, arguing that its larger brain and association with Oldowan tools justified placing it in the genus Homo. Fossils attributed to the species date from about 2.4 to 1.65 million years ago, with brain sizes averaging around 600 cm³. The oldest fossil assigned to the genus Homo, the LD 350-1 jaw from Ledi-Geraru in Ethiopia, is about 2.8 million years old. Researchers still debate whether habilis and the contemporary Homo rudolfensis belong in Homo or Australopithecus, and how they relate to Homo erectus.

title: Homo erectus appears
summary: A tall, long-legged human species with a larger brain emerged in Africa and became the first hominin known from fossils to spread widely across Asia.
description: Homo erectus had body proportions close to those of modern humans, adapted for long-distance walking and running, and a brain that grew from about 600 to more than 1,000 cm³ over its long existence. A braincase from Drimolen, South Africa, dated to about 2.04–1.95 million years ago, is among the oldest specimens, and the nearly complete 'Turkana Boy' skeleton from Nariokotome, Kenya, about 1.5 million years old, shows its tall, slender build. The species, or a group of closely related populations, spread to the Caucasus, China and Java and survived in Indonesia until about 110,000 years ago, making it the longest-lived human species known. Some researchers classify the early African forms separately as Homo ergaster.

title: Gigantopithecus, the largest known ape
summary: A giant relative of orangutans, known only from teeth and jaws, lived in the forests of southern China until changing habitats drove it extinct.
description: Gigantopithecus blacki was named by Ralph von Koenigswald in 1935 from huge molars he found among 'dragon teeth' sold in Hong Kong apothecary shops. Since then about 2,000 teeth and four lower jaws have been recovered from caves in Guangxi, southern China, beginning with a mandible from Liucheng in 1956; no other parts of the skeleton are known, so size estimates are speculative, though it may have weighed 200–300 kg. Proteins extracted from the enamel of a roughly 1.9-million-year-old tooth in 2019 confirmed that it was a close relative of orangutans. A 2024 study dated its extinction to between about 295,000 and 215,000 years ago, when more seasonal climates broke up its forests and it failed to adapt its diet, unlike the orangutans living alongside it.

title: Cryptid claims: surviving Gigantopithecus and megalodon
dateLabel: Claimed to survive today; youngest fossils c. 3.6 million (megalodon) and c. 215,000 years old (Gigantopithecus)
summary: Cryptozoologists claim Gigantopithecus survives as Bigfoot or the Yeti and that megalodon still lurks in the deep sea; scientists reject both claims.
description: Since the mid-twentieth century some writers have proposed that the Himalayan Yeti could be a surviving Gigantopithecus, and the anthropologist Grover Krantz argued from 1970 until his death in 2002 that North America's Bigfoot was one too, coining the name 'Gigantopithecus canadensis'. Supporters cite eyewitness reports, footprint casts and films such as the 1967 Patterson–Gimlin footage shot at Bluff Creek, California. Similar claims hold that megalodon survives unseen in the deep ocean, citing manganese-crusted teeth dredged up by HMS Challenger in 1873 that were once estimated to be only 11,000–24,000 years old. The idea was popularised by the 2013 Discovery Channel docufiction 'Megalodon: The Monster Shark Lives', whose supposed scientists were paid actors.
mainstreamView: No Gigantopithecus fossil is younger than about 215,000 years or comes from outside East and Southeast Asia, and no bones, bodies or verified DNA of Bigfoot or the Yeti exist; samples tested as Yeti remains have come from bears and other known animals, and the footprints and films are unverified or hoaxed. Megalodon's youngest fossils are about 3.6 million years old, it was a warm-water predator of coasts and open seas rather than a deep-sea animal, and a living population of giant sharks would leave abundant fresh teeth and bitten whale carcasses. The Challenger teeth look fresh because of their mineral crusts, whose growth rates cannot reliably date them.

title: Dmanisi: early humans outside Africa
summary: Five skulls from Dmanisi, Georgia, show that small-brained early humans had left Africa and reached the Caucasus about 1.8 million years ago.
description: Excavations beneath a medieval town in Georgia since 1991 have produced five skulls and other remains, along with Oldowan-style tools, dated to about 1.85–1.77 million years ago. The hominins were short, with brains of about 550–775 cm³, smaller than those of later Homo erectus, showing that the first dispersals out of Africa did not require large brains or Acheulean technology. The striking variation among the skulls, especially the complete Skull 5, led some researchers to argue that early Homo species such as habilis, rudolfensis and erectus were a single variable lineage, a view others dispute. Stone tools at Shangchen in central China, about 2.1 million years old, suggest that hominins had reached East Asia even earlier.

title: Acheulean hand axes
summary: Early humans in East Africa began shaping symmetrical, teardrop-shaped hand axes, a toolkit that would endure for over a million years.
description: The Acheulean, named after Saint-Acheul in northern France where such tools were described in the nineteenth century, is characterised by large bifacial tools, hand axes and cleavers, shaped by removing flakes from both faces. The oldest examples, from Kokiselei in West Turkana, Kenya, and Konso in southern Ethiopia, date to about 1.76–1.75 million years ago and are generally associated with Homo erectus. The technology spread across Africa, western Asia and Europe and persisted until roughly 200,000 years ago, making it the longest-lived tool tradition in human history, although hand axes are rare in East Asia. Their regular shapes imply planning and the teaching of skills between generations.

title: Java Man: Homo erectus in Southeast Asia
summary: Homo erectus reached Java, where Eugène Dubois's 1891 find at Trinil became the first known fossil of the species.
description: Searching deliberately for a 'missing link', the Dutch army surgeon Eugène Dubois found a skullcap and thigh bone at Trinil on the Solo River in 1891–92 and named them Pithecanthropus erectus, now Homo erectus. Later finds at Sangiran, a UNESCO World Heritage Site, show that hominins were present on Java by about 1.5 million years ago, although estimates range from about 1.7 to 1.3 million years. Java was often joined to mainland Asia when glacial sea levels were low. Homo erectus persisted on the island until about 117,000–108,000 years ago at Ngandong.

title: Mammoths and Ice Age megafauna spread
summary: Mammoths crossed the Bering land bridge into North America, part of a wave of large Ice Age mammals adapted to cold, open steppes.
description: Mammoths originated in Africa and spread into Eurasia around 3 million years ago, evolving into the steppe mammoth and later, in north-east Siberia, the woolly mammoth. They reached North America across Beringia about 1.5 million years ago, giving rise to the Columbian mammoth; DNA from Siberian mammoth teeth more than a million years old, published in 2021, suggests that the Columbian mammoth descended partly from a previously unknown lineage. Through the Pleistocene, every continent except Antarctica hosted outsized mammals, including woolly rhinos and giant deer in Eurasia, ground sloths and glyptodonts in the Americas, and Diprotodon and marsupial lions in Australia, most of which disappeared in the late Pleistocene.

title: Mid-Pleistocene Transition
summary: Ice-age cycles lengthened from about 41,000 to roughly 100,000 years and grew more extreme, without any matching change in Earth's orbit.
description: Deep-sea oxygen-isotope records and the thick loess and ancient soil sequences of China's Loess Plateau show that before about 1.25 million years ago glacial cycles followed the 41,000-year rhythm of changes in Earth's axial tilt. Over the next half-million years glaciations grew longer, colder and more intense, settling into a pattern of slow ice build-up and rapid melting roughly every 100,000 years. Because orbital forcing did not change, the cause must lie within the climate system; leading hypotheses include a gradual decline in CO2 and the stripping of soft regolith by earlier glaciations, which allowed thicker, more stable ice sheets to form on bedrock. The transition set the pattern of the late Pleistocene ice ages that modern humans lived through.

title: Earliest evidence of controlled fire
summary: Burned bone and plant ash deep inside Wonderwerk Cave, South Africa, are among the oldest widely accepted traces of fire used by early humans.
description: Microscopic analysis published in 2012 found ashed plant remains and burned bone in layers about 1 million years old, some 30 m inside Wonderwerk Cave, beyond the reach of wildfires, together with Acheulean tools. Older claims from Koobi Fora and Chesowanja in Kenya, at about 1.5 million years, are harder to distinguish from natural fires. At Gesher Benot Ya'aqov in Israel, clusters of burned flint suggest repeated fire use about 780,000 years ago, and habitual use of hearths is well documented from around 400,000 years ago at sites such as Qesem Cave in Israel and Beeches Pit in England. The primatologist Richard Wrangham has proposed that cooking helped drive the evolution of larger brains and smaller guts, an idea that remains debated.
wikipedia: Control of fire by early humans
mainstreamView: Fire use by about 1 million years ago is supported by the Wonderwerk Cave evidence and accepted by many researchers, but whether hominins could make fire or only harvested it from natural blazes is unknown. Claims older than 1 million years remain contested, and regular, habitual fire use is generally placed after about 400,000 years ago.

title: Homo antecessor at Atapuerca
summary: Fossils from Gran Dolina in northern Spain record some of the earliest humans in western Europe, with a face strikingly like ours.
description: Since 1994 the TD6 layer of the Gran Dolina cave in the Sierra de Atapuerca has yielded well over a hundred human fossils, dated to roughly 950,000–770,000 years ago and assigned in 1997 to a new species, Homo antecessor. Cut marks on many of the bones show that individuals, including children, were butchered and eaten. A juvenile face has a surprisingly modern-looking midface, and proteins from tooth enamel, analysed in 2020, place the species close to the common ancestor of Neanderthals, Denisovans and modern humans. Footprints at Happisburgh in England, about 950,000–850,000 years old, and a facial fragment from Atapuerca's Sima del Elefante, about 1.4–1.1 million years old, show that humans reached Europe even earlier.

title: Peking Man at Zhoukoudian
summary: Cave deposits near Beijing yielded remains of about 40 Homo erectus individuals; most of the original fossils were lost in 1941.
description: Excavations at Zhoukoudian from 1921, led after 1927 by Davidson Black, Pei Wenzhong and later Franz Weidenreich, recovered skullcaps, teeth and bones of Homo erectus, first named Sinanthropus pekinensis. Cosmogenic dating published in 2009 suggests that the oldest hominin-bearing layers are about 770,000 years old, older than once thought. The original fossils vanished in 1941 while being shipped for safekeeping during the Second World War and survive mainly as casts. Ash layers in the cave were long cited as evidence of controlled fire, but later analyses found that much of the material was not true ash, and fire use there remains debated.

title: Homo heidelbergensis: the Mauer jaw
summary: A jaw found in a sandpit near Heidelberg in 1907 gave its name to a widespread human species of the Middle Pleistocene.
description: The Mauer 1 mandible, discovered by a sandpit worker in 1907 and described by Otto Schoetensack in 1908, has been dated to about 609,000 years ago. The name Homo heidelbergensis has been applied to large-brained Middle Pleistocene humans across Africa and Europe, including fossils from Bodo in Ethiopia, Kabwe in Zambia and Petralona in Greece, and the species was long regarded as the common ancestor of Neanderthals and modern humans. Many of these populations made Acheulean hand axes and hunted large game, as shown by butchered horse and rhinoceros bones at Boxgrove in England, about 500,000 years old.
mainstreamView: The name is widely used, but its definition is contested. European fossils once assigned to it, such as those from Sima de los Huesos, are now often considered early Neanderthals; some researchers propose separate names, such as Homo bodoensis, for the African populations, while others doubt that the Mauer jaw can anchor a coherent species, a problem known as the 'muddle in the middle'.

title: Neanderthal and Denisovan lineages diverge
summary: Genomes from Denisova Cave in Siberia show that the ancestors of Neanderthals and Denisovans split from each other more than 400,000 years ago.
description: Analyses of high-quality genomes from Neanderthals and from a Denisovan finger bone found in Denisova Cave in the Altai Mountains indicate that the lineage leading to modern humans separated from the ancestors of both groups roughly 550,000–765,000 years ago, and that Neanderthals and Denisovans diverged from each other around 470,000–380,000 years ago. Nuclear DNA from the roughly 430,000-year-old Sima de los Huesos fossils in Spain, which already belong to the Neanderthal lineage, indicates that the split had happened before then. Neanderthals then spread across western Eurasia, while Denisovans, known mainly from DNA, a few teeth, a jaw from the Tibetan Plateau and a skull from Harbin in China, ranged across Asia. All three groups later interbred where they met. These dates depend on assumed mutation rates and generation times and are revised as methods improve.

title: Sima de los Huesos: early Neanderthals
summary: A deep pit in Spain's Atapuerca hills holds at least 28 people with early Neanderthal features, and some of the oldest human DNA ever recovered.
description: The 'Pit of the Bones', reached through the Cueva Mayor cave system, has yielded more than 6,000 human fossils from at least 28 individuals, dated to about 430,000 years ago. Their skulls and teeth show several Neanderthal traits, although their braincases remain more primitive. Nuclear DNA recovered in 2016 confirmed that they belong to the Neanderthal lineage, implying that Neanderthals and Denisovans had already separated by this time. How the bodies came to accumulate at the bottom of a 13 m shaft, possibly through deliberate deposition, is debated; a single red quartzite hand axe, nicknamed 'Excalibur', was found among them.

title: Homo naledi in the Rising Star Cave
summary: A small-brained human species with a mix of primitive and modern traits lived in South Africa at the same time as early members of our own lineage.
description: More than 1,500 fossil elements from at least 15 individuals have been recovered since 2013 from deep, hard-to-reach chambers of the Rising Star cave system near Johannesburg, in excavations led by Lee Berger. Homo naledi combined a brain of about 465–610 cm³ and curved fingers with human-like feet and hands. Yet its remains date to only about 335,000–236,000 years ago, overlapping with early Homo sapiens elsewhere in Africa. Claims published in 2023 that it deliberately buried its dead and engraved cave walls are contested by many researchers, who argue that the evidence for intentional burial and for the engravings' age and authorship is insufficient.
